summary: SELENARC is an interactive tool for comparing lunar south-pole landing sites and dates, and how mast height changes power and communication potential. Built for Lunar Landing Site Navigator, it combines NASA LOLA topography with JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions, shows both bodies against a terrain-derived horizon, and reports illumination, Earth visibility, and outages. Users place a solar-and-communications mast, change its location and height, and watch the windows recalculate. A discrete optimizer searches 130 configurations; under a 360-hour outage limit, 17 are feasible and it recommends a 5-meter mast. At Ridge A on Connecting Ridge (November 2026, 720 hours), modeled Earth visibility rises from 199 hours at the surface to 359.5 hours at 5 meters, and plateaus at 382 hours from 10 meters. Visibility is geometric line of sight only, not a link budget or power; Earth caps near 53% of the month due to libration.
details:
SELENARC helps mission planners, educators, and the public compare lunar south-pole landing sites and dates, and decide what minimum infrastructure improves a site's power and communication potential. Users start on a 3D Moon, fly to Connecting Ridge, place a solar-and-communications mast, change its location and height, and watch illumination, Earth visibility, and outage windows recalculate.

How it works

It combines NASA LOLA topography with JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions. For each candidate point it derives the terrain horizon and computes, hour by hour, when the Sun and Earth are above it. A discrete optimizer searches 130 site-and-mast configurations; under a 360-hour outage limit, 17 are feasible and it recommends a 5-meter mast.

Results

At Ridge A on Connecting Ridge (November 2026, 720 hours), modeled Earth visibility rises from 199 hours at the surface to 359.5 hours at 5 meters, and plateaus at 382 hours from 10 meters. An independent cross-check at Point B shows joint Sun+Earth visibility going from 0 hours at the surface to 297.5 hours with a 10-meter mast.

Benefits and impact

SELENARC turns raw terrain and ephemeris data into a clear, interactive answer: where to land, when, and how tall a mast needs to be. It makes south-pole planning understandable for non-specialists while staying traceable to NASA data.

Tools

Web app with an interactive 3D scene, Python and JavaScript analysis and tests, NASA LOLA data, and JPL Horizons, deployed on Vercel.

Limitations

Visibility is geometric line of sight only, not a link budget or a power model; Earth visibility caps near 53% of the month due to libration. Next step: extend the same pipeline to Artemis III candidate regions.
